claims.text: Adding approximately 3 vol% MoP precursor before quenching will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
The MoP precursor dissolves in the alloy during melting.
Rapid quenching of the MoP-containing melt nucleates nanoscale amorphous Mo–P-rich clusters.
Optimized mixing and quenching produce a uniform distribution of the Mo–P-rich clusters.
The amorphous Mo–P-rich clusters locally hinder atomic mobility.
The amorphous Mo–P-rich clusters act as pinning centers that inhibit the growth and propagation of crystalline nuclei.
Inhibition of crystalline growth by the clusters lowers the critical cooling rate required to obtain an amorphous alloy.
Inhibition of crystallization by the clusters raises the onset crystallization temperature during heating.
Melt-spinning at cooling rates of about 10^5–10^6 K/s can produce an amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
Cooling rate strongly affects the microstructure and phase composition of a phosphorus-containing multicomponent alloy.
Phosphorus can alter crystallization pathways and promote phosphide-rich phases in a complex multicomponent alloy.
The beneficial effect of MoP pre-alloying occurs only when the precursor is uniformly dispersed and forms appropriately sized amorphous clusters.
Excessive MoP precursor can cause macroscopic phase separation and negate the proposed improvements.
Cooling rates outside an optimized window can negate the proposed benefits of MoP pre-alloying.
TEM or atom-probe tomography should reveal a homogeneous population of nanoscale amorphous clusters in the modified alloy.
